messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] different posterior means from MCMC and HMC
parts:
See http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/hierarchical_2pl.html
for how to do this appropriately in Stan.  

As we have discussed many times on this list, you can’t just naively trust the
results that come out of software, especially older software like WinBUGS.
Statistically MCMC will not always return the right value, and even if it does
it might not do it unless you have millions of iterations.  The algorithms used
in Stan are more robust and also have many more diagnostics to check for
problems.  But ultimately the issue here is that you can’t compare the values,
let alone worry about discrepancies, until you have verified that the different
programs are returning reasonable values.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] different posterior means from MCMC and HMC
parts:
First of all, HMC is a form of MCMC, but I see you meant
Stan's HMC versus BUGS's conditional sampling (Gibbs if
everything's conjugate). More below.

> On Apr 25, 2017, at 1:09 PM, Ru Wang <wangr...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Thank you so much, Daniel. I used rstan to make estimation and my advisor used bugs to estimate. Our project wants to measure the true significance for the cases(14454) in the dataset. And there are 38 raters for each case, each will rating the case as significant(1) or nonsignificant(0).The attachments are the model for my project, data and my stan code. Actually, our model is not identifiable and the chains do not converge. To solve the identifiability problem, we adopt a normalization method after the estimation is complete.

Although Gelman and Hill recommended this in their regression
book, it won't work well in Stan because Stan's much better at mixing,
so it'll run away in a single iteration.
> As you can see from the attachment. And after transformation, the chains converge.

It's better to write an identifiable model in the first place. Posterior
transformations of badly behaved chains isn't guaranteed to work or give
you a proper solution even if the transformed parameters do appear to
converge. The problem is that all the guarantees only hold if you're
sampling from a proper posterior.

Of course, we can't help you with specifics without more detail. But
I can tell you that I've spent a lot of time working on these rating
problems and your model is deficient in that it doesn't adjust for the
biases of the raters, which has been substantial in all the examples I've
studied. What you want to do is have a latent true value for
each item then paramters corresponding to sensitivity and specificity of
each rater. There's an example in the Stan manual of the Dawid and Skene
model for general multinomial responses---it's even easier with just
binary responses.

If there are I items and J raters, and y[n] is the annotation
or rater jj[n] on item ii[n], then the model you want involves a latent
true value z[n]. Then z[n] has a distribution given prevalence phi:

z[n] ~ bernoull(phi);

and then

y[n] ~ bernoulli(theta[jj[n], z[ii[n]]]);

where theta[j, 0] is one minus annotator j's specificity and
theta[j, 1] is annotator j's sensitivity. And you can put some
hierarchical priors on the theta[, 0] and theta[, 1]. You can also add
random effects and other predictors. I have a tutorial on these
models that goes through the binary case and even includes WinBUGS
code (this was the class of model that led me to quit natural language
processing and take up statistics):

https://lingpipe.files.wordpress.com/2008/04/malta-2010-slides.pdf

Of course, Stan indexes from 1 and you need to marginalize out the
z, but otherwise, these models fit really well.

- Bob
